JPL-2005-06-06.note: Same release text is also served at .../nasas-opportunity-rover-rolls-free-on-mars-3/ (the supplied R4 link) with the date July 15, 2005. Release number shown on the -3 page: 2005-400. Use the June 6 page as the publication date; the release describes drives through June 4.

R5-Cooper-2006.author: Brian Cooper
R5-Cooper-2006.note: Written 18 months after Purgatory; describes general practice and techniques developed over time.

R6-JPL-Edu.published: not captured in Sprint 0 (page concerns the 2019 mission end)

claims.wording: April 26, 2005 · Sol 446
claims.support: Both captions: 'its 446th martian day, or sol (April 26, 2005)'.

claims.wording: Meridiani Planum, about 2 km south of Endurance Crater
claims.support: PIA07216: 'about 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) south of Endurance Crater at a place known informally as Purgatory Dune'. PIA07999: 'Mars' Meridiani Planum region'.

claims.wording: The ripple was about a third of a metre tall and 2.5 m wide.
claims.support: 'about one-third meter (one foot) tall and 2.5 meters (8 feet) wide'.
claims.use: Hero ripple reference dimensions; caption. Not a survey of the whole map.

claims.wording: Its wheels dug more than 10 cm into soft sand.
claims.support: PIA07999: 'dug more than 10 centimeters (4 inches) deep'. PIA07922 and May 6 release: 'dug itself (in) to wheel-hub depth'. June 6 release: 'all six wheels ... mired up to their rims'.
claims.note: Three phrasings. Runtime model wheel radius is 0.131 m (rig-metadata.json), so hub depth is about 13 cm and agrees with 'more than 10 cm'. The sink-versus-command curve is a tuning parameter.

claims.wording: Opportunity had covered nearly 40 m of a planned 90 m drive when its wheels began to slip.
claims.support: 'had completed nearly 40 meters (131 feet) of a planned 90-meter (295-foot) drive that sol when its wheels began slipping'.
claims.use: Replay-segment caption. The in-game approach is shorter and must be labelled compressed.

claims.wording: The rover was driving backwards, a routine practice that spread lubricant in its wheels.
claims.support: 'The rover was driving backwards at the time. The rover team frequently alternates between backwards and forwards driving to keep wheel lubrication well distributed.'

claims.wording: The wheels kept turning, but the rover hardly moved. After a turn that did not work, it stopped itself.
claims.support: 'The wheels kept rotating enough times to have covered the rest of the distance ... but the rover eventually barely inched forward. After a turn at the end of the planned drive, Opportunity sensed that it had not turned properly and stopped moving.'
claims.note: 'inched forward' has an ambiguous frame because the rover was driving backwards. Do not use the word 'forward' for this moment.

claims.wording: Opportunity had crossed dozens of similar ripples. This one was a little taller and steeper.
claims.support: Maimone, May 6: 'We've climbed over dozens of ripples, but this one is different in that it seems to be a little taller and to have a steeper slope, about 15 degrees on part of its face'. June 6: 'dozens of similar ones the rover easily crossed'. PIA07216: nearby features 'only about 10 to 15 centimeters ... tall'.
claims.note: 15 degrees is reported for part of one face. Use it as a shape reference, not a physics constant.
claims.use: Level design: practice ripples low and crossable, hero ripple taller

claims.wording: The team sent no wheel commands until testing on Earth was done.
claims.support: May 6: 'The team has not asked Opportunity to turn its wheels at all since the rover bogged down'. PIA07922: 'more than a week designing and conducting tests'.

claims.wording: Engineers built a sand trap on Earth and practised with a test rover. Ordinary sand gave too much grip, so they mixed a finer, powdery soil.
claims.support: May 6: test rover 'had no difficulty driving away' in existing sand; recipe of play sand, diatomaceous earth and mortar clay powder; 'more than 2 tons'; material 'fills the gaps between the cleats'.
claims.note: The mix is an Earth analogue chosen for behaviour. It is not a statement about Martian soil composition.

claims.wording: From May 13 to June 4 the team sent short, cautious drives and checked each result.
claims.support: 'The rover team directed the drives in cautious increments from May 13 through June 4.' Biesiadecki: 'patiently followed the strategy developed from the testing, monitoring every step of the way'.

claims.wording: The wheels turned enough to drive 192 m. The rover moved about 1 m.
claims.support: 'the rover churned 192 meters (629 feet) worth of wheel rotations before gaining enough traction to actually move one meter'.
claims.note: Different interval from PG-13. Never combine them or turn either into a game traction formula.

claims.wording: In eight drives over 11 days the rover advanced 26 cm while its wheels turned enough for 46 m.
claims.support: 'starts on Opportunity's 460th martian day, or sol (May 10, 2005) and ends 11 days later. In eight drives during that period, Opportunity advanced a total of 26 centimeters ... 46 meters'.
claims.note: The pack's recovery notes say 'sols 460-471'. The caption does not give an end sol; that range is a derived conversion and should not be printed.

claims.wording: Getting free took more than five weeks.
claims.support: PIA07999: 'more than five weeks of planning, testing, and carefully monitored driving'.
claims.discrepancy: June 6 release: 'worked diligently for nearly five weeks to extricate the rover'. R6: 'worked for five weeks'. R7: 'free Opportunity in June 2005 after six weeks'. PIA07216: 'stuck ... for more than a month'. April 26 to June 4 is 39 days (my arithmetic), which fits 'more than five weeks' and not 'six weeks'.
claims.use: Time-compression label. Do not show a 'Week 6' counter.

claims.wording: By June 4, 2005 Opportunity was back on firmer ground.
claims.support: Drives 'through June 4'; PIA07999 taken 'sol 491 (June 11, 2005), a week after the rover drove safely onto firmer ground'.
claims.unresolved: The sol number for June 4 is not stated in any source checked. Do not print one.

claims.wording: Opportunity crept back along its own tracks to firmer ground.
claims.support: Image observation on the pack originals: in PIA07999 (sol 491) the tracks stop at the trench heads and nothing continues beyond them, so entry and exit tracks lie on the same side of the trap.
claims.note: Verified by image observation, not by a text statement. Board crops: lookback-far.jpg.
claims.use: Escape caption; recovery direction on the map (north)

claims.wording: (no player text) The rover left with its front leading.
claims.support: Entered rear-first (PG-06, text). Model front is the mast and arm end. PIA07922: mast end faces the entry tracks on sol 446. PIA07216: sundial end faces away from the tracks while stuck. PIA07999: sundial end faces the trap after escape. With PG-16a this gives front-leading travel on the way out.
claims.inference: Chassis-forward recovery. R6's 'backed out' describes the retreat, not reverse gear.
claims.unresolved: No text source states the chassis-relative direction. Assumes the rover did not turn around while mired; the sundial observations support that.
claims.use: Recovery animation; FORWARD and REVERSE command tiles (level-blueprint.md section 2)

claims.wording: (do not use as a fact)
claims.support: R6: 'Its right front wheel dug into loose sand, reaching to just below its axle' and 'turned its stuck wheel just the right amount and backed out'.
claims.discrepancy: The 2005 primary accounts describe all six wheels mired (June 6) and wheel-hub depth for the rover (May 6, PIA07922), not one stuck wheel. No source gives a steering angle or a wheel-specific command.
claims.use: None. Steering during recovery is a tuning parameter of a simplified puzzle. The team brief's 'the real fix: turn the stuck wheel a little and back out slowly' needs rewording.

claims.wording: Each approach was tested on Earth before commands were sent to Mars.
claims.support: June 6: 'We did careful testing ... Then we patiently followed the strategy developed from the testing'. R6: 'Engineers tested their commands repeatedly with consistent results'.

claims.wording: One rover planner wrote the commands. A second checked them. Only then were they sent.
claims.support: 'Rover Planner One ... writes command sequences ... Rover Planner Two checks the sequences ... Only then are the sequences sent to a rover.'

claims.wording: A radio signal needed about ten minutes to cross between Earth and Mars.
claims.support: R5: 'It takes ten minutes or more for a radio signal to travel between Earth and Mars' (general). June 6: 'From about 174 million kilometers away'.
claims.note: 174 million km divided by the speed of light is about 9.7 minutes one way (my arithmetic), so 'ten minutes or more' is slightly too strong for June 2005. Use 'about ten minutes' or 'minutes'.
claims.use: Why you plan instead of steering live

claims.wording: (optional) Later drives added checks that stop the rover if it starts to slip.
claims.support: 'Over time, we developed new techniques ... We do slipchecks to verify that the rover is not stuck'.
claims.note: R5 does not say when slip checks began relative to Purgatory. Do not show them as available before the trap.

claims.wording: Afterwards the team studied the ripple to plan safer drives.
claims.support: 'Opportunity's next task is to examine the site ... After we analyze this area, we'll be able to plan safer driving in the terrain ahead'.

claims.wording: Planned mission: 90 sols and about 1,000 m of driving.
claims.support: 'Designed to last just 90 Martian days and to travel 1,100 yards (1,000 meters)'.

claims.wording: By April 2005 Opportunity had already worked a year past its planned mission.
claims.support: 'for more than a year of extended missions since successfully completing their three-month primary missions in April 2004'.

claims.wording: When Opportunity fell silent in 2018 it had driven 45.16 km.
claims.support: 'When it fell silent in 2018, Opportunity had run up 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers)'; 'When NASA declared the mission complete on Feb. 13, 2019, total rover odometry was 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers)'.
claims.note: The team brief pairs 45.16 km with 'years spin to 2017'. That pairing is not supported. No intermediate odometer reading has been sourced, so the montage must not show one.

claims.wording: Opportunity exceeded its planned lifetime 60 times over.
claims.support: 'exceeding its life expectancy by 60 times'. Key dates on the same page: landing Jan. 24, 2004; last communication June 10, 2018; end of mission Feb. 13, 2019.
claims.note: 'About 15 years' fits landing to end of mission. Landing to last contact is about 14.4 years (my arithmetic). Prefer NASA's '60 times' or name both dates.

claims.wording: (SAND and OVERTIME link text for Spirit rover and Ingenuity)
claims.support: Not checked in Sprint 0. R6 partly supports Spirit: 'in 2009 ... Spirit got stuck on a slope ... Its mission officially ended in 2011'; it does not say 'Troy' or 'soft sand'.
claims.use: Reward text in Sprint 4. Check the NASA sources listed for F-35 to F-37 in TEAM_CONTEXT.md first.

claims.wording: (visual direction, no player text)
claims.support: 'approximately true-color rendering' from 750, 530 and 480 nm filters; lighting varied over nine sols; seams smoothed in the sky; tracks and some crests 'dustier than the undisturbed' soil.
claims.note: Palette authority for ground and horizon. The sky is smoothed, so it is a weaker reference for sky gradients.

claims.wording: (asset measurement, no player text)
claims.support: Normalized bounds 2.28 m wide, 1.65 m long, 1.58 m tall. Wheel radius 0.131 m. Front and rear wheel centres 1.06 m apart across and 1.21 m apart along the body. Wheel width 0.161 m. Mast at z -0.46 to -0.28 and arm at z -0.50 to -0.22, with -Z as the front (GLB accessor bounds).
claims.note: Measured from the project's converted NASA model, not from a NASA dimension sheet.

claims.wording: (design reference, no player text)
claims.support: Tick labels on the image run from -10.0 to +10.0 at 100 px spacing: 1 cm per pixel, 20 x 20 m, centred on the camera mast. Track gauge reads 0.92 to 1.04 m against 1.06 m on the model.
claims.note: Read directly from the pack original. The caption does not state the mosaic's compass orientation.
claims.use: Scale for all plan readings (M-01, M-02)

claims.wording: (design reference, no player text)
claims.support: Crests are sinuous with junctions and dead ends, 2 to 4 m apart, running within roughly 10 to 20 degrees of the track direction. The last crest crossed lies 3.5 to 4 m before the stuck mast, crossed at roughly 40 degrees.
claims.note: Visual readings, about +/-0.3 m. Not a survey.
claims.use: Ripple field parameters; L-last-crest placement (M-03 to M-05)

claims.wording: (design reference, no player text)
claims.support: No rocks, outcrops or hills are visible to the horizon in either image.

claims.wording: (design reference, no player text)
claims.support: Mean encoded values in fixed boxes: sky #d8ae76, undisturbed ground #4d3521 to #563a23, churned track #75482a. Churned material is brighter, redder and cloddy.
claims.note: Study samples of an 'approximately true-color' JPEG; not calibrated colours. Boxes are in resource-catalog.json.
claims.use: Material targets and rejection criteria 5 and 6 (M-08)
